title: Anti-GBM, Double Positives and ANCA-Negative Vasculitis
summary: Learn the target and linear immunofluorescence of anti-GBM disease, why every anti-GBM patient also needs an ANCA test, what dual MPO plus PR3 positivity suggests, how EGPA differs by ANCA status, and why a negative ANCA does not exclude vasculitis.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 54 Hits 4, 11 and 13 and Trap 2. Checked against McAdoo and Pusey 2025 (anti-GBM treatment standard), Kozmar 2025 (ANCA testing recommendations), Lyons 2019 (EGPA by ANCA status), Weng and Liu 2019 (drug-induced AAV) and Jin 2018 (levamisole-adulterated cocaine). The reviewer’s “treat before serum creatinine exceeds 5 mg/dL” is not a cutoff in the source: kidney outcome falls with presenting creatinine above 500 µmol/L (about 5.7 mg/dL) and especially with dialysis dependence, and treatment is still recommended for selected dialysis-dependent patients and always for lung haemorrhage; see register flag rv-anti-gbm-creatinine-cutoff. Not taught as fact: the 11–17%/9–16% seronegativity figures, “capillaritis” and “myocarditis without vasculitis” in the EGPA split, and the Number Vault anti-GBM incidence and assay figures.

objectives: State the target antigen and immunofluorescence pattern of anti-GBM disease, and why ANCA should also be tested.
Recognise dual MPO plus PR3 ANCA positivity as a clue to drug-induced vasculitis.
Explain why a negative PR3/MPO-ANCA result does not exclude ANCA vasculitis, including ANCA-negative EGPA.

scenes.title: Three sera, three puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three sera reach the immunology bench. (1) A 68-year-old with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and haemoptysis: anti-GBM positive AND MPO-ANCA positive. (2) A cocaine user with purpura: MPO-ANCA positive AND PR3-ANCA positive. (3) A patient with asthma, eosinophilia and neuropathy whose PR3 and MPO immunoassays are both negative. Question token: “Two antibodies, or none: what next?”

cues.text: Three sera reach the bench. An older patient with failing kidneys and coughed-up blood is positive for anti-GBM and for MPO-ANCA.
A cocaine user with purpura is positive for both MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA. And a patient with asthma, eosinophilia and neuropathy is negative for both.
Two antibodies, or none: what does each pattern mean, and what comes next?

props.label: Two antibodies, or none: what next?

scenes.title: Anti-GBM disease: a straight line of IgG
scenes.altText: Schematic glomerulus. Target card: anti-GBM autoantibodies (IgG) recognise the non-collagenous domain of the α3 chain of type IV collagen, α3(IV)NC1, in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes. Disease card: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis in more than 90% of classic cases and alveolar haemorrhage in 40–60%. Diagnosis card: linear, ribbon-like IgG along the GBM on immunofluorescence of frozen kidney tissue is the diagnostic gold standard; circulating anti-α3(IV)NC1 antibody is found in more than 90% of classic cases, and commercial immunoassays have high sensitivity and specificity.

cues.text: Anti-GBM disease is caused by IgG autoantibodies against one target: the non-collagenous domain of the alpha-3 chain of type four collagen, in the basement membranes of glomeruli and lung alveoli.
The result is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, and in roughly forty to sixty percent of classic cases, bleeding into the lungs.
On kidney biopsy, immunofluorescence of frozen tissue shows a strong linear, ribbon-like band of IgG along the basement membrane. That is the diagnostic gold standard.
In the blood, circulating antibody is found in more than ninety percent of classic cases, and commercial immunoassays are highly sensitive and specific.

scenes.title: Double positives and the dialysis line
scenes.altText: Double-positive card: circulating ANCA, usually anti-MPO, occurs in 30–40% of anti-GBM disease. Double-positive patients have the age profile of ANCA vasculitis and more chronic biopsy lesions, but present with the severe features of anti-GBM disease and receive standard anti-GBM treatment first; they relapse at a rate comparable to ANCA vasculitis (single-positive anti-GBM rarely relapses, under 3%), so they need maintenance immunosuppression. Outcome card (one long-term cohort treated with plasma exchange, cyclophosphamide and glucocorticoids): renal survival 95% at 1 year and 94% at 5 years with presenting creatinine below 500 µmol/L (about 5.7 mg/dL), versus 82% and 50% above it; only 8% of dialysis-dependent patients recovered independent kidney function at 1 year. Dialysis status at the start of treatment is the strongest determinant of kidney outcome.

cues.text: Anti-GBM disease often brings a second antibody. ANCA, usually against MPO, is found in thirty to forty percent of cases. So when anti-GBM is positive, test for ANCA too.

Double-positive patients present as severely as anti-GBM disease and are treated the same way first. But they relapse like ANCA vasculitis, whereas single-positive anti-GBM disease rarely relapses, so they need maintenance treatment.

Speed matters. In one long-term cohort, kidney survival at five years was ninety-four percent when the presenting creatinine was below five hundred micromoles per litre, about five point seven milligrams per decilitre, but fifty percent above it.
Only eight percent of patients already on dialysis recovered kidney function at one year. Dialysis status at the start of treatment is the strongest predictor.

scenes.title: Two ANCAs, or none
scenes.altText: Dual-ANCA card: in primary ANCA vasculitis, ANCA generally recognise only one target, MPO or PR3; in antithyroid-drug-induced disease ANCA typically recognise several neutrophil antigens, and dual PR3 plus MPO positivity is described as characteristic of levamisole-adulterated cocaine vasculitis. Drugs linked to drug-induced ANCA vasculitis include propylthiouracil, hydralazine, minocycline, D-penicillamine and cocaine/levamisole; stopping the drug is central to management. EGPA card: ANCA (mainly MPO) is found in only about a third to a half of EGPA. The MPO-positive group has more glomerulonephritis and neuropathy (vasculitic features); the ANCA-negative group has more lung infiltrates and cardiac involvement. Hook answers: (1) double-positive anti-GBM: anti-GBM treatment plus maintenance; (2) MPO + PR3: take a drug history, including cocaine; (3) negative immunoassays with high suspicion: IIF, then an alternative immunoassay; ANCA-negative EGPA is common.

cues.text: In primary ANCA vasculitis, the antibodies usually see one target: MPO or PR3. Positive for both? Think of drugs. Dual positivity is characteristic of vasculitis from levamisole-adulterated cocaine.
Other linked drugs include propylthiouracil, hydralazine, minocycline and penicillamine. Stopping the drug is central to treatment.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is ANCA-positive in only about a third to a half of patients, mainly MPO. MPO-positive patients have more glomerulonephritis and neuropathy; ANCA-negative patients have more lung infiltrates and heart involvement.

Back to the hook: the double-positive patient is treated as anti-GBM disease, then maintained; the dual-ANCA patient needs a drug history; and the negative serum, with high suspicion, goes on to further testing.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “ANCA-negative rules out ANCA vasculitis” (✓ with negative PR3/MPO immunoassays and high clinical suspicion, do IIF on ethanol-fixed, preferably also formalin-fixed, neutrophils, then consider an alternative immunoassay; ANCA-negative EGPA is common); “Anti-GBM positive, so skip ANCA” (✓ 30–40% are double-positive, which changes long-term treatment); “MPO plus PR3 = two separate vasculitides” (✓ dual positivity points to drug-induced disease).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative ANCA rules out ANCA vasculitis. No: with high suspicion, go on to immunofluorescence and an alternative immunoassay, and remember many EGPA patients are ANCA-negative.
Trap two: anti-GBM is positive, so ANCA is not needed. No: thirty to forty percent are double-positive, and they need maintenance treatment.
Trap three: MPO plus PR3 means two diseases. No: dual positivity points to a drug, such as levamisole-adulterated cocaine.

props.title: ✗ “ANCA − rules out AAV.”
lines: ✓ High suspicion: IIF, then another assay

scenes.title: One antibody, one story
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “One antibody tells one story. A second antibody means a second chapter: anti-GBM plus ANCA is a story that can come back (relapse); MPO plus PR3 is a story written by a drug; and no antibody is not the end of the book.” Tokens: GBM + ANCA = relapse risk · MPO + PR3 = drug · none ≠ excluded. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: one antibody tells one story. Anti-GBM plus ANCA is a story that can come back. MPO plus PR3 is a story written by a drug. And no antibody is not the end of the book.

Where it breaks: not every drug-induced case is dual-positive, and antithyroid-drug cases are mostly MPO only; double positives are still treated first as anti-GBM disease; and assay performance differs between methods.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Anti-GBM: linear IgG to α3(IV)NC1 · always test ANCA (30–40% double-positive) · dialysis status predicts kidney outcome”, “MPO + PR3 → drug history · ANCA-negative does not exclude AAV or EGPA”.

cues.text: Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG against type IV collagen and needs an ANCA test because about a third are double-positive, while dual MPO and PR3 positivity points to a drug and a negative ANCA never excludes vasculitis when suspicion is high.

props.label: Anti-GBM: linear IgG · test ANCA too (30–40%) · dialysis predicts outcome
MPO + PR3 → drug history · ANCA − does not exclude AAV/EGPA

explanation.what: Plain language: in anti-GBM disease, antibodies attack a collagen in the kidney and lung filters and line up in a straight line on biopsy. Many of these patients also carry ANCA. Two different ANCAs at once is a characteristic clue that a drug caused the disease, and a negative ANCA test does not prove there is no vasculitis. Scientific terms: anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody, α3(IV)NC1, linear IgG immunofluorescence, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN), alveolar haemorrhage, double-positive disease, MPO-ANCA, PR3-ANCA, drug-induced ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), indirect immunofluorescence (IIF).
explanation.why: Double-positive anti-GBM patients relapse like ANCA vasculitis and need maintenance therapy, so missing the ANCA changes care. Primary AAV usually targets one antigen, so a second specificity is a clue to a drug trigger. A negative PR3/MPO immunoassay does not exclude AAV: recommendations call for further methods when suspicion is high, and much of EGPA is ANCA-negative.
explanation.measure: Anti-GBM: circulating antibody in > 90% of classic cases; linear IgG on frozen-tissue IF is the gold standard; ANCA co-positivity 30–40%, mostly MPO; relapse < 3% for single-positive. Kidney survival in one cohort: 95%/94% at 1/5 years with creatinine < 500 µmol/L vs 82%/50% above; 8% of dialysis-dependent patients recovered at 1 year. EGPA: ANCA positive in about 30–50%. Negative PR3/MPO with high suspicion: IIF on ethanol-fixed (preferably also formalin-fixed) neutrophils, then an alternative high-quality immunoassay.
explanation.differs: Single-positive vs double-positive anti-GBM (rare relapse vs AAV-like relapse); primary AAV (one antigen) vs drug-induced AAV (several antigens, dual MPO + PR3); MPO-positive EGPA (glomerulonephritis, neuropathy) vs ANCA-negative EGPA (lung infiltrates, cardiac involvement).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the anti-GBM target or IF pattern, choose the additional test for an anti-GBM-positive patient, link dual MPO + PR3 to a drug, or pick the next step after negative ANCA immunoassays with high suspicion.

mnemonic.text: One antibody tells one story. A second antibody means a second chapter: anti-GBM plus ANCA is a story that can come back; MPO plus PR3 is a story written by a drug; and no antibody is not the end of the book.
mnemonic.explanation: Double-positive anti-GBM = relapse risk; dual ANCA = drug clue; negative ANCA ≠ excluded.
mnemonic.limitation: Not every drug-induced case is dual-positive (antithyroid-drug cases are mostly MPO only); double positives are still treated first as anti-GBM disease; assay performance differs between methods.

analogyLimitations: Glomerulus and antibody drawings are schematic.
Outcome figures come from one long-term cohort quoted in a review; other series differ.
takeaway: Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG against type IV collagen and needs an ANCA test because about a third are double-positive, while dual MPO and PR3 positivity points to a drug and a negative ANCA never excludes vasculitis when suspicion is high.

questions.stem: A patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis has a kidney biopsy showing linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Which additional serological test is most important to request?

options.rationale: Correct. 30–40% of anti-GBM patients are also ANCA-positive (mostly MPO); double positives relapse like ANCA vasculitis and need maintenance therapy.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM antibodies are not a common finding in lupus, and anti-dsDNA does not detect the ANCA co-positivity (30–40%) that changes long-term treatment.

options.text: No further test; the biopsy is diagnostic
options.rationale: Incorrect. The biopsy confirms anti-GBM disease but does not show whether ANCA is also present.
Incorrect. Rheumatoid factor does not detect the ANCA co-positivity that changes long-term treatment in anti-GBM disease.

questions.stem: A serum is positive for both MPO-ANCA and PR3-ANCA by immunoassay. Which history is most relevant?

options.text: Use of cocaine, which may be adulterated with levamisole
options.rationale: Correct. Dual PR3 plus MPO positivity is characteristic of drug-induced vasculitis, including levamisole-adulterated cocaine.
Incorrect. A sore-throat history does not explain dual MPO plus PR3 positivity, which the sources link to drug-induced vasculitis.

options.text: A family history of granulomatosis with polyangiitis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Primary ANCA vasculitis usually has one target antigen, so family history does not explain dual positivity.
Incorrect. Vaccination is not the association the sources describe for dual MPO plus PR3 positivity; drugs are.

questions.stem: A patient with high clinical suspicion of ANCA vasculitis is negative on PR3- and MPO-ANCA immunoassays. What is the best next laboratory step?

options.text: IIF on ethanol-fixed (preferably also formalin-fixed) neutrophils, then consider an alternative high-quality immunoassay
options.rationale: Correct. This is the recommended path when immunoassays are negative but suspicion is high.

options.text: Report that ANCA vasculitis is excluded
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative immunoassay with high suspicion calls for further methods, and ANCA-negative disease, including ANCA-negative EGPA, exists.

options.text: Repeat the same immunoassay daily until positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. The recommendation is to move to a different method (IIF, then an alternative immunoassay), not to repeat the same one.

options.text: Measure anti-GBM instead and stop ANCA testing
options.rationale: Incorrect. Anti-GBM testing is recommended alongside ANCA in pulmonary-renal syndrome, but it does not replace further ANCA testing.

ANCA co-positivity 30–40%, double-positive behaviour and maintenance; relapse rare in single-positive disease.
Kidney survival by presenting creatinine (500 µmol/L) and dialysis dependence.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says to treat anti-GBM disease before serum creatinine exceeds 5 mg/dL. The treatment standard read here gives no such cutoff: outcome worsens above a presenting creatinine of 500 µmol/L (about 5.7 mg/dL) and especially with dialysis dependence, and intensive treatment is still recommended for alveolar haemorrhage regardless of kidney function and for selected dialysis-dependent patients.
